learn: All matter is made of particles far too small to see, even with a regular microscope.
Evidence for particles: when sugar dissolves in water, it seems to disappear, but the water tastes sweet, so the sugar particles are still there.
Air is matter too. Inflating a ball shows that air particles take up space and have mass.
check: Why does dissolved sugar still taste sweet?
lessons.try: Weigh a deflated ball, pump it up and weigh it again.

lessons.t: Particles in Solids, Liquids and Gases
learn: In solids, particles are packed tightly and vibrate in place.
In liquids, particles are close but slide past each other.
In gases, particles are far apart and move freely and quickly.
lessons.try: Act out solid, liquid and gas particles with a group of people.

learn: Diffusion is when particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are less crowded.
A drop of food colouring spreads through water without stirring.
Diffusion is faster in warm water because particles move faster.
lessons.try: Drop food colouring in hot and cold water and compare.

learn: Properties used to identify materials include colour, hardness, reflectivity, electrical and thermal conductivity, magnetism and solubility.
Mass is measured with a balance in grams. Volume can be measured with a graduated cylinder.
Each material has a set of properties that helps identify it.
check: Volume of a liquid can be measured with a...
lessons.try: Test five household materials for magnetism and whether they dissolve in water.

learn: Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume.
Objects less dense than water float; denser objects sink.
A large log floats while a small pebble sinks, because wood is less dense than water.
check: Density is mass packed into a...
Wood is less dense than water
lessons.try: Predict and test whether ten objects float or sink.

learn: A mixture combines substances that keep their own properties, like trail mix or sand and iron filings.
A solution is a mixture where one substance dissolves evenly in another, like salt water.
Mixtures can be separated by physical means: filtering, magnets or evaporation.
check: How can you separate salt from water?
lessons.try: Separate a mixture of sand, salt and paper clips.

units.t: Physical Changes, Chemical Changes and Conservation of Mass

learn: A physical change alters size, shape or state but not what the substance is.
Melting ice, tearing paper and dissolving sugar are physical changes.
Many physical changes can be reversed.
lessons.try: List five physical changes you see at home.

learn: A chemical change creates new substances with new properties.
Signs include a new colour, a gas forming, light or heat being given off, or a solid forming in a liquid.
Rusting iron, baking bread and burning wood are chemical changes. Most can't be reversed.
check: Which is a sign of a chemical change?
lessons.try: Watch a cut apple turn brown over an hour and explain why it's a chemical change.

learn: In both physical and chemical changes, the total mass stays the same.
When ice melts, the water has the same mass as the ice.
In a sealed container, mass before and after a change is equal. If gas escapes an open container, the measured mass seems to drop.
check: Melted ice has ___ mass as the ice.
Why might mass seem to drop in an open container?
lessons.try: Weigh an ice cube in a sealed bag, let it melt, and weigh it again.

units.t: How Plants Get What They Need

learn: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis.
They use light energy, water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air to make sugar, releasing oxygen.
Most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
check: Most of a plant's mass comes from...
lessons.try: Put a water plant in a glass of water in sunlight and watch for oxygen bubbles.

learn: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil.
Xylem tubes carry water up to the leaves; phloem carries sugars to the rest of the plant.
Water evaporates from leaves through tiny openings called stomata.
lessons.try: Put a clear plastic bag over a plant leaf and watch water collect.

learn: Scientists test one variable at a time to see what plants need.
Keep other conditions the same (controlled variables) for a fair test.
Measure height, leaf count or colour as data.
lessons.try: Design an experiment testing the effect of light on bean plant growth.

units.t: Food Webs and the Flow of Energy

learn: Producers, like plants, make their own food using sunlight.
Consumers eat other organisms: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both.
Decomposers, like fungi and bacteria, break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
check: An animal that eats both plants and animals is...
lessons.try: Classify ten organisms as producers, consumers or decomposers.

learn: A food chain shows one path of energy: grass → rabbit → fox.
A food web shows many connected food chains in an ecosystem.
Arrows point in the direction energy flows, toward the eater.
check: In a food chain, arrows point toward...
In grass → rabbit → fox, the rabbit is...
lessons.try: Draw a food web for a pond ecosystem.

learn: Nearly all energy in food webs began as sunlight captured by producers.
The energy in animals' food is used for body warmth and motion.
Changes to one part of a food web can affect many other organisms.
check: Most energy in food webs comes from...
lessons.try: Predict what would happen to a food web if all the rabbits disappeared.

learn: Earth has four major systems: the geosphere (rock and soil), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things).
Each system interacts with the others.
Rain (hydrosphere) erodes mountains (geosphere); plants (biosphere) add oxygen to the atmosphere.
lessons.try: Find an example of each sphere interacting in your neighbourhood.

learn: Wind (atmosphere) shapes sand dunes (geosphere).
Ocean currents (hydrosphere) affect climate (atmosphere).
Animals (biosphere) dig burrows that change soil (geosphere).
check: Wind shaping sand dunes is the atmosphere and the...
lessons.try: Draw a diagram showing three interactions between Earth's spheres.

learn: Scientists use models to study Earth systems, like terrariums or computer simulations.
A terrarium models how water cycles between soil, plants and air.
Models help predict changes.
check: Cycles between soil, plants and air
lessons.try: Build a sealed terrarium and observe the water cycle inside.

learn: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans.
Only about 3% is fresh water, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps.
Less than 1% of Earth's water is fresh water we can easily use from lakes, rivers and groundwater.
check: About how much of Earth's water is salt water?
Frozen in glaciers and ice caps
lessons.try: Model Earth's water with 100 cups: 97 salty, 2 frozen, 1 usable.

learn: Water evaporates from oceans and lakes, rising as water vapour.
Vapour condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation.
Water collects in bodies of water or soaks into the ground as groundwater.
check: Water soaking into the ground becomes...
lessons.try: Draw and label the water cycle.

learn: Scientists graph the amounts of water in different places.
A pie chart can show the percentage of salt water, ice and fresh water.
Graphs help people understand why fresh water must be protected.
check: Graphs help people understand why fresh water must be...
Which graph best shows parts of a whole?
lessons.try: Make a pie chart of Earth's water.

learn: People's activities affect land, water and air.
Farming, cities and mining change habitats. Pollution harms water and air.
Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.
check: Burning fossil fuels adds ___ to the atmosphere.
lessons.try: List three ways your community affects the environment.

learn: People can reduce impacts: recycling, conserving water, using renewable energy and protecting habitats.
Communities build parks, plant trees and clean up waterways.
Laws like the Clean Water Act (1972) protect resources.
check: The Clean Water Act was passed in...
lessons.try: Calculate how much water you save by turning off the tap while brushing.

learn: Engineers design solutions such as water filters, solar panels and wildlife crossings.
Wildlife crossings let animals cross highways safely.
Engineers test designs and improve them.
check: A sand and gravel filter makes water...
Clearer, but not safe to drink
lessons.try: Design a simple water filter using sand, gravel and cotton (do not drink the water).

units.t: Gravity and the Sun as a Star

learn: Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward the centre of Earth.
That's why "down" is toward Earth's centre everywhere on the planet.
Gravity acts on all objects, and heavier objects don't fall faster when air resistance is small.
check: Do heavier objects fall faster without air resistance?
lessons.try: Drop two balls of different mass at the same time and compare.

learn: The Sun is a star, a huge ball of hot gas.
It looks bigger and brighter than other stars because it's much closer: about 150 million kilometres away.
Other stars are so far away that their light takes years to reach us.
check: Why does the Sun look brighter than other stars?
It is the biggest star in the universe
It is hotter than all stars
About how far is the Sun from Earth?
lessons.try: Compare how big a ball looks up close and far away.

learn: A star's apparent brightness depends on its size, temperature and distance.
Some stars are much larger and brighter than the Sun but look dim because they're far away.
Astronomers measure distances in light-years, the distance light travels in a year.
check: Apparent brightness depends on size, temperature and...
Some huge stars look dim because they are...
lessons.try: Shine two flashlights from different distances and compare brightness.

learn: Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, causing day and night.
The Sun appears to move from east to west because Earth turns.
Shadows change length and direction during the day.
check: Day and night are caused by...
lessons.try: Measure a stick's shadow every hour on a sunny day.

learn: Earth revolves around the Sun once every 365 1/4 days.
Earth's tilted axis causes seasons: the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer.
Different stars are visible in different seasons.
check: Earth revolves around the Sun in about...
The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has...
lessons.try: Use a lamp and a tilted ball to model the seasons.

learn: The Moon orbits Earth about every 29.5 days, showing phases: new, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full.
Phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half.
Constellations are patterns of stars, like Orion, that seem to move across the sky through the year.
check: The Moon's phases repeat about every...
Different amounts of the sunlit half
lessons.try: Observe the Moon for two weeks and draw its phases.
